name: AI Devices in Europe: MDR, IVDR and the AI Act
blurb: The two regimes an AI device must satisfy in the EU.
title: AI Devices in Europe: MDR, IVDR and the AI Act
answer: In Europe an AI medical device must meet the Medical Device or In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation and, where it needs notified body review, the AI Act's requirements for high risk systems: data quality, robustness, transparency, human oversight and cybersecurity. Guidance has started to align the two so a single conformity assessment can cover both.

reading.body:
An AI medical device sold in Europe must satisfy the Medical Device Regulation or the In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation, and the AI Act as well where notified body review is required.

The two regimes overlap rather than stack. The AI Act's high risk obligations cover data quality, robustness, transparency, human oversight and cybersecurity, and those are the same properties a notified body already examines under MDR or IVDR. Guidance has begun to align the two so one conformity assessment can serve both.

For a medtech team the practical consequence is that the AI Act work belongs inside the existing quality system, not beside it. A parallel compliance track duplicates evidence that the device regulator is already collecting. The AI Act entered into force on 1 August 2024 and treats AI medical devices needing notified body assessment as high risk.

What this does not cover is timing. The data gives no dates for when the high risk obligations begin to apply to devices, no detail on how the aligned assessment is conducted, and no view of devices that fall outside notified body review. It also says nothing about compute, hosting or the physical infrastructure a device runs on, so no conclusion about those can be drawn from it.

sections.body: Run AI Act requirements through the existing MDR quality system rather than building a parallel one.
